Question: What protein, encoded by a gene located on chromosome 14, can cause excessive elastin breakdown in the aorta and potentially elevate the risk of developing an abdominal aortic aneurysm when deficient?
 Answer: alpha-1 antitrypsin
 Referece:
 Zeroshot - O3 
 Detailed explanation: The SERPINA1 gene, situated on chromosome 14q32, encodes the serine-protease inhibitor alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT). AAT’s main physiological role is to neutralize neutrophil elastase and related proteases. When AAT is deficient, elastase activity in connective-tissue–rich organs, including the aortic wall, is left unchecked, leading to excessive degradation of elastin fibers. This accelerated elastin breakdown weakens the aortic media and has been associated with a higher incidence of abdominal aortic aneurysm formation. Thus, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency can promote pathological elastin loss in the aorta and elevate AAA risk.

746202:
Question: Does familial intestinal polyatresia syndrome (FIPA) increase Rho kinase activity, thereby disrupting the polarity?
 Answer: yes
 Referece:
 Zeroshot - O3 
 Detailed explanation: Familial intestinal polyatresia syndrome (FIPA) is most commonly caused by loss-of-function mutations in the TTC7A gene. TTC7A normally restrains the RhoA/ROCK (Rho-associated co-iled-coil-containing protein kinase) pathway. When TTC7A is defective, RhoA becomes hyper-activated, which in turn increases ROCK kinase activity. Elevated ROCK signaling perturbs the organization of the actin cytoskeleton, leading to failure of apical-basal polarity in intestinal epithelial cells. Restoration of polarity in experimental models can be achieved by pharmacologic inhibition of ROCK, confirming that excessive ROCK activity is the proximal driver of the polarity defect. Therefore, FIPA is indeed associated with increased Rho kinase activity that disrupts epithelial polarity.

Question: What drug can be used to enrich hair cells by heightening blood supply in fair-haired children with a hair disorder?
 Answer: minoxidil
 Referece:
 Zeroshot - O3 
 Detailed explanation: Fair-haired children may present with loose anagen hair syndrome, a disorder in which the anagen (growing) hairs are poorly anchored and shed easily. One therapeutic approach is to improve follicular nutrition by increasing scalp blood flow. Minoxidil, originally an antihypertensive arterial vasodilator, is applied topically for this purpose. By dilating dermal blood vessels, minoxidil raises local blood supply, delivering more oxygen and nutrients to the hair matrix cells, thereby stimulating thicker, stronger anagen hairs. Clinical reports document successful use of 2–5 % topical minoxidil in fair-haired children with this condition, making minoxidil the drug of choice to enrich hair cells through enhanced vascular perfusion.

Question: Does a condition related to ODD syndrome affect the functioning of the ring and middle fingers?
 Answer: yes
 Referece:
 Zeroshot - O3 
 Detailed explanation: Oculodentodigital dysplasia (often abbreviated ODD or ODDD) is a genetic syndrome caused most commonly by pathogenic variants in the GJA1 gene. One of its hallmark skeletal manifestations is syndactyly—partial or complete fusion—of the central digits of the hand. The fusion most frequently involves the third and fourth fingers (middle and ring) and/or the fourth and fifth fingers (ring and little). Because the affected digits are joined and may also exhibit camptodactyly, clinodactyly, or shortened phalanges, patients typically experience restricted independent motion, reduced grip dexterity, and other functional limitations of those fingers. Hence, a condition related to ODD syndrome does indeed affect the functioning of the ring and middle fingers.

 Detailed explanation: The aortopulmonary space (often referred to as the aortopulmonary window) contains lymph nodes and loose connective tissue situated between the aortic arch and the main pulmonary artery. Any pathological process that produces lymph-node enlargement or soft-tissue masses in the mediastinum can therefore manifest in this space.  
• Infections (e.g., tuberculosis, fungal infections, bacterial lymphadenitis) can cause reactive or suppurative enlargement of mediastinal lymph nodes, including those in the aortopulmonary window.  
• Autoimmune or granulomatous disorders such as sarcoidosis, IgG4-related disease, or rheumatoid nodules can similarly lead to nodal or soft-tissue involvement in this region.  
• Malignancies—whether primary mediastinal tumors (lymphoma) or metastatic disease (e.g., lung, breast, melanoma)—commonly produce aortopulmonary window lymphadenopathy or mass lesions.  
Therefore, infectious, autoimmune, and neoplastic conditions are all well-recognized causes of abnormal findings in the aortopulmonary space.

When the body lacks vitamin A, epithelial cells lose their ability to mature properly and instead become hyper-keratinized, a change clinically referred to as hyperkeratosis or follicular keratosis. This process involves excessive synthesis and deposition of keratin—a scleroprotein—within the affected epithelial layers. The resulting overproduction and accumulation of keratin is a well-documented hallmark of vitamin A deficiency, manifesting in dry, rough skin, keratinised conjunctival plaques (Bitot spots), and other keratinisation disorders. 627609:
Question: Is it true that yellow fever is one of the only two viral hemorrhagic fevers with an available vaccine, and that a single dose offers lifelong immunity, even in symptomatic HIV-positive individuals?
 Answer: no
 Referece:
 Zeroshot - O3 
 Detailed explanation: Two parts of the statement are incorrect. (1) Yellow fever is not “one of only two” viral-hemorrhagic fevers (VHFs) with a vaccine. In addition to yellow fever, licensed or routinely used human vaccines now exist for several other VHFs—e.g., Ebola virus disease (Ervebo, 2019), dengue (Dengvaxia, 2015), Argentine hemorrhagic fever (Candid #1, used since the 1990s in Argentina), and Kyasanur Forest disease in India. Thus yellow fever is not uniquely one of just two VHFs with an available vaccine. (2) While the World Health Organization states that a single dose of the 17D yellow-fever vaccine provides lifelong protection for immunocompetent persons, this does NOT apply to symptomatic HIV-positive individuals. Because the vaccine is live-attenuated, it is contraindicated in patients with advanced or symptomatic HIV infection or severe immunosuppression (typically CD4 < 200 cells/µL); those who are eligible but immunocompromised may mount a weaker response and may require re-vaccination or repeated serologic testing. Therefore the claim that one dose confers lifelong immunity “even in symptomatic HIV-positive individuals” is not supported by current medical consensus.

Question: Is ionizing radiation a risk factor of both brain cancer and chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML)?
 Answer: yes
 Referece:
 Zeroshot - O3 
 Detailed explanation: Extensive epidemiologic and experimental evidence shows that exposure to ionizing radiation increases the incidence of several malignancies, including both brain tumors and chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML). 

1. Brain cancer: Survivors of therapeutic cranial irradiation for conditions such as tinea capitis or childhood leukemia, as well as atomic-bomb survivors and patients who received high-dose diagnostic/therapeutic radiation to the head, have a clearly elevated risk of primary brain tumours (e.g., gliomas, meningiomas). This association has been consistently reproduced and accepted as causal by authoritative bodies such as the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) and the U.S. National Academies’ BEIR committees.

2. Chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML): Ionizing radiation is a well-documented leukemogenic agent. Cohorts of atomic-bomb survivors, radiotherapy patients, and occupationally exposed workers show an increased incidence of CML that rises with cumulative radiation dose. CML is one of the classic hematologic malignancies listed among the radiation-induced cancers by the United Nations Scientific Committee on the Effects of Atomic Radiation (UNSCEAR) and other expert reviews.

Because ionizing radiation is an established, dose-related risk factor for both primary brain cancers and CML, the statement is correct.

Question: Which parasitic disease affects the central nervous system in 10-24% of cases of cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, a rare type of stroke caused by blood clots in the brain's venous sinuses?

 Referece:

 Detailed explanation: Paragonimiasis is the tissue-fluke infection produced by Paragonimus species (most often Paragonimus westermani). Although the adult worms characteristically lodge in the lungs, aberrant migration occurs in a substantial proportion of patients. Epidemiologic series show that 10 – 24 % of documented Paragonimus infections involve ectopic sites, most commonly the brain or spinal cord, giving rise to cerebral (neurologic) paragonimiasis. When the parasite lodges in the central nervous system it can provoke seizures, focal deficits, intracranial inflammation and, on occasion, thrombotic complications such as cerebral venous sinus thrombosis – a rare form of stroke produced by clotting of the brain’s dural venous sinuses. Therefore, the parasitic disease whose central-nervous-system involvement is seen in roughly 10–24 % of affected individuals and is linked to CVST is paragonimiasis.

736626:
Question: Can MacDermot-Winter syndrome, prenatal alcohol exposure, and vertically transmitted infections cause microcephaly?
 Answer: yes
 Referece:
 Zeroshot - O3 
 Detailed explanation: All three factors listed are recognized causes of microcephaly.

1. MacDermot-Winter syndrome (also termed blepharophimosis-ptosis-microcephaly syndrome) is a rare genetic disorder whose core diagnostic triad includes congenital microcephaly, characteristic eyelid malformations, and developmental delay. Thus, microcephaly is an intrinsic feature of the syndrome.

2. Prenatal alcohol exposure, particularly the spectrum encompassed by fetal alcohol syndrome, disrupts brain growth during gestation. A consistent hallmark of this teratogenic exposure is reduced head circumference at birth and throughout childhood, i.e., microcephaly.

3. Vertically transmitted (congenital) infections—classically grouped as TORCH (toxoplasmosis, “other” such as syphilis and Zika, rubella, cytomegalovirus, herpes) and similar pathogens—can cross the placenta, injure the developing fetal brain, and result in structural abnormalities, including microcephaly. Recent outbreaks of congenital Zika infection dramatically underscored this causal link.

Therefore, MacDermot-Winter syndrome, prenatal alcohol exposure, and vertically transmitted infections are all established etiological factors capable of causing microcephaly.

 Answer: corpus callosotomy
 Referece:
 Zeroshot - O3 
 Detailed explanation: Foix–Chavany–Marie syndrome (opercular syndrome) can occasionally be produced not by permanent structural lesions but by bilateral propagation of epileptic discharges that transiently inactivate the frontal opercular cortices.  When the epilepsy is medically intractable, disconnective surgery that prevents the rapid spread of ictal activity from one hemisphere to the other can abolish the opercular seizures and the associated negative motor phenomena.  Corpus callosotomy – sectioning the corpus callosum either partially (usually the anterior two-thirds) or completely – is a well-established neurosurgical treatment for refractory epilepsy.  By interrupting interhemispheric spread, a callosotomy can eliminate the bilateral opercular involvement, leading to complete resolution of the Foix–Chavany–Marie syndrome that was being produced by those epileptic discharges.  Case reports document full recovery of voluntary facial, lingual, pharyngeal and masticatory movements after corpus callosotomy in such patients, confirming the effectiveness of this procedure in reversing FCMS when it is seizure-induced.

Question: Does the effect of alpha 1-antitrypsin deficiency on connective tissue integrity increase the risk of developing an abdominal aortic aneurysm?
 Answer: yes
 Referece:
 Zeroshot - O3 
 Detailed explanation: Alpha-1-antitrypsin (AAT) is the principal circulating inhibitor of neutrophil elastase. When AAT is deficient, unchecked elastase activity degrades elastin and other structural proteins that are critical for connective-tissue integrity in the lung, liver and vascular walls. Several epidemiological studies and case series have reported a higher prevalence of arterial aneurysms—including abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA)—in individuals with severe AAT deficiency (e.g., Pi*ZZ genotype) compared with the general population. Experimental work also demonstrates increased aortic elastin fragmentation and dilatation in AAT-deficient animal models. Taken together, the established mechanism (protease–antiprotease imbalance leading to elastin degradation) and supportive clinical data indicate that AAT deficiency does increase susceptibility to AAA formation. Therefore, the effect of AAT deficiency on connective-tissue integrity is considered a risk factor for developing an abdominal aortic aneurysm.
